title: Kindness Insulted: War with Ammon and Aram
summary: When the Ammonite king Nahash dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun, but Hanun's officials accuse them of spying, and Hanun humiliates them. The Ammonites hire Aramean chariots and troops, and Joab and Abishai defeat the combined armies near Rabbah. When the Arameans regroup under Hadadezer's commander Shophach, David leads Israel across the Jordan and defeats them, and the Arameans make peace and stop helping Ammon.
story: Chapter 18 summarized David's victories in broad strokes; this chapter slows down to tell one campaign in detail. It explains how the war with Ammon, mentioned briefly in 18:11, began, and it fills in how Hadadezer's Arameans became David's subjects. It also sets the scene for chapter 20, where Joab besieges the Ammonite capital, Rabbah. The chapter parallels 2 Samuel 10. In Samuel, the siege of Rabbah frames the story of David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11-12). The Chronicler will pass over that story, keeping his focus on the kingdom and the preparations for the temple.
historical:
Ammon was a small kingdom east of the Jordan, centered on Rabbah (on the site of modern Amman, Jordan). Its king Nahash had once besieged Jabesh-gilead and been defeated by Saul (1 Samuel 11). The Bible does not say what kindness Nahash showed David; many suggest he helped David while Saul was pursuing him, since Nahash was Saul's enemy, but the text is silent. The Ammonites hired chariots and troops from Aramean states to the north: Aram-naharaim (upper Mesopotamia), Aram-maacah (a small state near Mount Hermon), and Zobah. Medeba, where the hired forces camped, lay on the plateau south of Rabbah.

The numbers differ from 2 Samuel 10. There the hired troops are twenty thousand foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, a thousand men with the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand men of Tob, a total of thirty-three thousand; here verse 7 speaks of thirty-two thousand chariots. Verse 18 has seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers, where 2 Samuel 10:18 has seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen. Copying errors in numbers were common in ancient manuscripts, and scholars also note that the Hebrew word often translated thousand can sometimes mean a military unit.
cultural:
Sending envoys to console a new king on his father's death was standard diplomacy, a way of reaffirming a treaty relationship with the next ruler. Hanun's officials read it as espionage, a real danger since envoys could scout defenses. The humiliation was severe. In that world a full beard marked a man's honor and maturity, and shaving it by force was a deep disgrace (2 Samuel 10:4 says half of each beard was shaved). Cutting their garments at the hips exposed them, a shame associated with the treatment of prisoners. David's instruction to stay in Jericho until their beards grew back spared them further public shame.

The Ammonites realized they had become a stench to David, an idiom for having made themselves odious and provoked hostility. Hiring foreign chariot forces with a thousand talents of silver shows how the smaller states of the region bought military power; a talent was the largest unit of weight, commonly estimated at around thirty kilograms.
literary: The chapter moves in three acts: the insult (verses 1-5), the first battle (verses 6-15), and the second battle (verses 16-19). Each act turns on seeing and hearing: the princes' suspicion, the Ammonites seeing they had become odious, Joab seeing battle lines before and behind, the Ammonites seeing the Arameans flee, the Arameans seeing they had been defeated. At the center stands Joab's speech (verses 12-13), a short and memorable call to mutual help and courage that ends in trust: May the LORD do what is good in His sight. The ending neatly reverses the beginning. The Ammonites hired the Arameans to help them; by the end the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore.

outline.t: Joab and Abishai fight on two fronts
The Arameans regroup and are defeated by David

doctrines.note: Joab fights hard and plans well, but leaves the outcome with God: May the LORD do what is good in His sight (verse 13). Human effort and trust in God's will stand together.
Suspicion turns a gesture of kindness into a war. The chapter traces how pride and fear in Hanun's court escalated into disaster for Ammon and its allies.

words.note: Chesed, kindness or loyal love. David wants to show chesed to Hanun because his father showed chesed to him (verse 2). In relations between kings the word describes loyalty within an alliance. The same word describes God's covenant love in chapters 16 and 17.

Nacham, to comfort or console. David's envoys come to console Hanun (verses 2-3). In other contexts the verb can mean to relent or be sorry, as in 21:15, where God relents from judgment. Here it is the ordinary word for condolence.

Chazaq, to be strong. Joab uses it in his speech, be strong (verse 13), and also for the enemy being too strong (verse 12). The call to strength recurs in Chronicles, as when David tells Solomon to be strong and courageous (22:13).

christ: The chapter's direct link to Christ is thin, and it is better to say so than to force one. There is a thematic contrast worth noticing. David's kindness was offered in good faith and met with suspicion and contempt, and the result was war. In the gospel, God's kindness in Christ is also met with rejection, yet God answers not with retaliation but with the cross, making peace through the blood of Christ (Colossians 1:20). Joab's call to fight and then leave the outcome to God also echoes a pattern of faithful action combined with trust that the New Testament commends.
questions: Hanun's advisers read the worst motive into a kind act. Where are you tempted to assume bad motives, and what might it cost?
Joab and Abishai agreed to help each other depending on which side was pressed hardest. What does that kind of mutual support look like among friends or in a church?
Joab said, May the LORD do what is good in His sight, after making every plan he could. How do you hold effort and trust together?
